script.opening: “Hi, thanks for calling back. It’s about my baby, Rayan — he’s four months. He’s had a cold since the weekend, but since yesterday he’s coughing a lot and his breathing sounds really noisy, sort of crackly and fast. My daughter had the same cold. Is it just a cold? Should I be giving him Calpol?”

facts.text: If asked: “Runny nose started Saturday — so three days. The cough and the noisy breathing started yesterday afternoon and it’s worse today.”

If asked to describe or listen: “It’s fast — faster than normal. I can see his tummy going in and out a lot. I don’t think his ribs are sucking in, I’m not sure what that looks like.” If the doctor explains how to look under the vest: “Oh… yes, there’s a little dip under his ribs when he breathes.” No grunting noise. If asked to count breaths for a minute while the doctor times it: “I got fifty-eight.”
“His colour looks okay now. Pink. His lips are pink.”

facts.topic: Pauses / colour change (HIDDEN — only if asked directly)
facts.text: Hesitates, then: “Actually… last night, about 3 o’clock, he sort of stopped breathing for a few seconds. His lips looked a bit blue-grey, then he coughed and started again. I thought I might have imagined it — I was half asleep. It hasn’t happened since, that I’ve seen.”
If asked: “He’s bottle-fed. Normally he has about 150 ml every three to four hours. Since last night he’s only taking 60 or 70 ml before he gets tired and pulls off. He sweats a bit while feeding.”
“Only two wet nappies since last night — normally it’s six or so in a day. They’re not soaked.”
“He’s sleepier than normal but he wakes up and cries properly. He did smile at me this morning.” Not floppy. Cry is normal, not weak or high-pitched.
“I checked with the ear thermometer — 37.9 this morning. I haven’t given anything yet.”
“He brought up a bit of milk once after coughing. No rash. No diarrhoea.”
“He came at 36 weeks, a bit early. He didn’t need special care — we went home after two days. His jabs are up to date. No heart problems or anything that I know of.”
“My husband Imran is at work — he’s a bus driver, he can’t just leave. I don’t drive. My daughter Mariam is three, she’s here with me. My mum lives ten minutes away.”
If asked: “I don’t think I had the RSV one in pregnancy — I had the whooping cough one.”

Calm and articulate at first, getting more anxious as the call goes on. Do not mention the breathing pause unless asked directly about pauses, stopping breathing, going blue or colour change. If asked, disclose it with embarrassment. If the doctor advises an ambulance, first resist (“Is that really necessary? He seems okay now”) and raise Mariam and having no car; accept once the reason is explained clearly and a plan for Mariam is agreed (her mum can come over). If the doctor is dismissive or rushed, become quieter and agree to everything without understanding.

ice.ideas: “I think it’s the cold my daughter had — maybe a chest infection. He might need antibiotics or some medicine for the breathing.”
ice.concerns: Underneath: she is frightened by what she saw at 3 am but worried she will be judged as an over-anxious mum or will “waste an ambulance”. She also worries about who will look after Mariam.
ice.expectations: Advice about Calpol and maybe a prescription; she does not expect to be told he needs to go to hospital.

cues: “He’s sleepier than normal” — said quickly, then moves on.
Slight hesitation when asked “anything else you’ve noticed?” — “No… I don’t think so.” (The pause in breathing is behind this.)
“My husband can’t just leave work” — a practical barrier she raises if hospital is mentioned.

checkpoints.text: Assesses breathing effort remotely and specifically — rate (asks the parent to count for a minute), visible recession, grunting, colour — and explains how to look
Asks directly about pauses in breathing or colour change (apnoea / cyanosis) and identifies the reported apnoea
Quantifies feeding (about half of usual volume) and wet nappies, and asks about alertness, temperature and risk factors (age, prematurity, heart or lung disease)
Recognises reported apnoea as a reason for immediate emergency referral (999 ambulance) and does not offer a home-care or next-day plan
Gives safe interim advice while waiting — stay with him, keep him upright for feeds, what to do if he stops breathing or goes blue again, bring the red book
Documents and hands over — informs the team/duty doctor as per local process and arranges a follow-up call or check that the ambulance has been called
Explores her worries and the practical barriers (no car, 3-year-old at home) and helps solve them rather than ignoring them
Explains the likely diagnosis (bronchiolitis) and why an ambulance is needed in plain language without frightening or blaming her; checks understanding

worked.txt: “Thank you for ringing — you were right to call. Tell me about Rayan from the start.”
“Could you lift his vest so you can see his tummy and chest? I’ll time a minute — count each time his tummy rises. And look just under his ribs — is the skin sucking in with each breath?”
“Has there been any time he has stopped breathing, even for a few seconds, or gone blue or grey around the lips?”

“It sounds like bronchiolitis — a common virus that affects babies’ small airways. Most babies get through it at home, but a pause in breathing changes things. Babies his age can have more pauses, so I need him checked in hospital now, and the safest way is an ambulance.”
“Can your mum come round for Mariam, or come with you? I’ll stay on the line while you ring 999 — or I can arrange it from here.”
“While you wait: keep him with you and watch his breathing. If he stops breathing or goes blue, tell the 999 call handler straight away — they will guide you.”

f.learning: In a baby with bronchiolitis the remote consultation turns on a few questions: breathing effort (rate, recession, grunting), colour, feeding (under 50–75% of usual), wet nappies, alertness, and risk factors (under 3 months, prematurity especially under 32 weeks, chronic lung or significant heart disease, neuromuscular disease, immunodeficiency). Apnoea — observed OR reported — is a reason for immediate emergency referral even if the baby seems settled now; a reassuring voice on the phone does not cancel it. Parents rarely volunteer a pause in breathing, so ask directly. Home management (small frequent feeds, saline drops, paracetamol only for distress with fever, no antibiotics, salbutamol or steroids) is only right when red flags have been asked about and are absent, with clear safety-netting. Being honest about the limits of a telephone assessment and solving practical barriers (transport, siblings) are part of safe management.

timeMap.d: Let mum tell the story. Confirm who you are speaking to and that the baby is with her.
Guide her to count breaths and look for recession; colour; grunting; pauses or blue spells; feeds as a fraction of usual; wet nappies; alertness; temperature; prematurity and other risk factors.
Bronchiolitis is likely; the reported pause in breathing means emergency referral now. Say it clearly.
Solve transport and childcare; agree who rings 999 (or arrange it); interim advice; what to tell the call handler.
Check understanding, document, inform the team and agree a follow-up check.

wordPics.clearPass: Takes a structured remote history with the mother as the eyes and ears, asks directly about pauses and colour change, quantifies feeding and nappies, recognises reported apnoea as a 999 trigger, explains bronchiolitis and the reason for the ambulance kindly, and solves the childcare and transport problem so the plan actually happens.
wordPics.pass: Identifies the apnoea and feeding drop and arranges emergency assessment, with reasonable explanation; practical barriers are addressed but less fully, or the remote assessment is less structured.
wordPics.fail: Assesses only some features and either misses the apnoea or recognises it but offers a delayed or same-day surgery appointment instead of emergency transfer; explanation is unclear or rushed.
wordPics.clearFail: Gives home-care advice (Calpol, fluids, “ring back if worse”) or antibiotics without asking about apnoea, feeding or breathing effort; dismisses the mother’s worry; no safe plan.

avoid.dont: “It’s just a cold — babies get lots of them. Give him Calpol and ring back if he gets worse.”
avoid.instead: “Most coughs at this age are viral, but I need to ask some specific questions about his breathing and feeding before I can say how to look after him.”
avoid.why: Reassurance before assessing severity misses the red flags that change the plan.

avoid.dont: “Did he stop breathing? Probably not, if he’s fine now.”
avoid.instead: “Thank you for telling me — that’s really important, and you were right to mention it.”
avoid.why: Reported apnoea is a red flag even when the baby looks well afterwards; minimising it shuts the parent down.

avoid.dont: “Take him to A&E when you can.”
avoid.instead: “Because of the pause in his breathing, the safest way is an ambulance now — let’s sort out Mariam together.”
avoid.why: A vague instruction with no plan for the barriers often leads to delay.

model.text: Hello, is that Aisha? It’s Dr Lewis from the surgery, calling back about Rayan. Is he with you now, and is now an okay time to talk?
model.why: Confirms identity, that the baby is present, and readiness

model.text: Yes, he’s here on my lap. He’s got a cough and his breathing sounds noisy — is it just a cold?
Tell me what’s been happening from the beginning.
Runny nose since Saturday, then since yesterday this cough and fast, crackly breathing. My daughter had the same cold.
I can’t see him, so I’d like you to be my eyes. Can you lift his vest? I’ll time a minute — count each time his tummy rises. And look just below his ribs: does the skin suck in with each breath?
model.why: Structured remote assessment of rate and recession, with clear instructions

model.text: Fifty-eight… and yes, there’s a little dip under his ribs.
Thank you, that’s really helpful. Is he making a grunting noise at the end of each breath? And what colour are his lips and tongue?
No grunting. His lips are pink now.
Has there been any time he has stopped breathing, even for a few seconds, or gone blue or grey around the mouth?
model.why: Asks directly about apnoea — the hidden red flag

model.text: Actually… last night, about three, he stopped for a few seconds and his lips looked bluey-grey, then he coughed and started again. I thought I might have imagined it.
I’m really glad you told me — that’s important, and you haven’t done anything wrong. How is his feeding compared with normal, and how many wet nappies today?
model.why: Validates and continues to quantify feeding and hydration

model.text: He’s only taking 60 or 70 ml instead of 150, and only two wet nappies since last night. He was born at 36 weeks.

From what you describe, Rayan probably has bronchiolitis — a common virus that inflames the tiny airways in babies’ lungs. Most babies manage at home, but a pause in breathing, together with him feeding half his usual amount, means he needs to be checked in hospital now. The safest way is an ambulance.
model.why: Names the diagnosis and gives a clear emergency decision with the reason

model.text: An ambulance? He seems okay now. And I’ve got my daughter here, and my husband’s at work.

I understand — it feels a big step when he looks settled. The worry is that pauses can happen again, and in hospital they can watch his breathing and oxygen and help with feeds. Could your mum come for Mariam, or come with you both?
model.why: Acknowledges the concern, explains the risk, and works on the practical barrier

model.text: My mum’s ten minutes away. I’ll ring her.

Ring 999 now and tell them he is 4 months old with bronchiolitis and stopped breathing for a few seconds last night. Keep him with you, upright if he coughs. If he stops breathing or goes blue again, tell the call handler straight away — they’ll talk you through what to do. Bring his red book.
model.why: Specific interim safety advice and what to say to 999

model.text: Okay. Should I give him Calpol for the temperature?

You can if he seems uncomfortable — the dose for his age is on the bottle, but please don’t delay the call for it. I’ll ring you back in 20 minutes to check the ambulance is on its way, and I’ll note this in his records for the hospital team. Can you tell me what you’re going to do now?
Ring 999, ring my mum, and tell them about the pause.
Exactly. You’ve done the right thing calling us today.
model.why: Supportive close that removes the fear of being judged

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children: diagnosis and management (2015, updated 2021) · UKHSA Green Book chapter 27a: RSV (maternal vaccination programme since September 2024)
knowledge.summary: Bronchiolitis is a viral lower respiratory tract infection, usually RSV, in children under 2 (most often under 1). Diagnose clinically. The key primary care task is deciding who can stay at home: refer immediately for emergency care for apnoea (observed or reported), looking seriously unwell, severe respiratory distress (grunting, marked recession, rate over 70/min), central cyanosis or persistently low oxygen saturation.

points.t: Coryzal prodrome for 1–3 days, then persistent cough with tachypnoea or recession, and wheeze or crackles. Fever is usually under 39 °C; high fever suggests another cause such as pneumonia.
Apnoea (observed or reported), seriously unwell appearance, severe respiratory distress (grunting, marked chest recession, respiratory rate over 70/min) or central cyanosis.

Respiratory rate over 60/min; feeding difficulty or inadequate fluid intake (50–75% of usual, using clinical judgement); clinical dehydration; persistent oxygen saturation under 92% on air. Lower the threshold with risk factors.

Under 3 months, prematurity (especially under 32 weeks), chronic lung disease, haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, neuromuscular disorders, immunodeficiency. Also consider distance from hospital and parental confidence.

On the phone the parent is your eyes: ask them to count breaths for a full minute, look for recession under the ribs, listen for grunting, check lip and tongue colour, and quantify feeds and wet nappies. Be explicit when you cannot assess safely remotely.

Small frequent feeds, saline nose drops if feeding is difficult, paracetamol or ibuprofen only for fever with distress. Do not use antibiotics, salbutamol, ipratropium, steroids or montelukast. Symptoms peak around days 3–5 and the cough can last 3–4 weeks.
Give clear advice: call 999 for pauses in breathing, blue colour or severe struggling to breathe; seek urgent review for reduced feeds, fewer wet nappies, worsening breathing or a very sleepy baby.
RSV vaccination is offered in pregnancy from 28 weeks to protect babies in their first months.

social.t: Transport, siblings and a partner at work are common reasons for delay. Solving them is part of the management plan, not an afterthought.

legal.t: A parent with parental responsibility can consent for a 4-month-old. Record who you spoke to.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice expects you to recognise and work within the limits of a remote consultation. If you cannot be sure a baby is safe, arrange face-to-face assessment at the right level of urgency, and document your reasoning.

community.t: NHS “Bronchiolitis” pages and local “When should I worry?” leaflets give parents a traffic-light guide for the following days.

redFlags: Pauses in breathing or blue/grey colour — ask directly
Grunting, marked recession, very fast breathing
Feeds under half to three-quarters of usual; few wet nappies
Very sleepy, floppy, weak or high-pitched cry
psychosocial: Who is at home; transport; siblings
ice: Idea: “just a cold” or a chest infection
Concern: worried about being judged as over-anxious
Expectation: Calpol advice or a prescription

playbook.diagnosis: Probable bronchiolitis with reported apnoea and reduced feeding in a 4-month-old born at 36 weeks — needs emergency hospital assessment.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It sounds like bronchiolitis, a common virus that swells the tiny breathing tubes in babies’ lungs. Most babies are fine at home, but the pause in his breathing means he needs checking in hospital straight away.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought it was the same cold as Mariam’s, and you were right that it started that way — but the pause in his breathing is the bit that needs hospital.”
management.psychosocial: Plan childcare with grandmother; reassure that calling was the right thing; avoid any sense of blame.
sharedPlan: What to tell the call handler
Bring red book; grandmother to look after Mariam
safetyNet: If he stops breathing or goes blue: tell 999 immediately
GP call-back in 20 minutes to confirm the ambulance is coming
Document and inform the duty team

pitfalls.intro: This station is about one question most candidates forget to ask. The baby “sounds okay” on the phone; the mother saw something at 3 am that changes everything.

items.fail: Never asking about pauses in breathing or colour change.
items.why: Reported apnoea is an emergency referral trigger, and parents rarely volunteer it.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Has he ever stopped breathing, even for a few seconds, or gone blue or grey?”

items.why: Feeding under 50–75% of usual and few wet nappies are the commonest reasons for admission.
items.fix: Ask “how many ml normally, and how many now?” and “how many wet nappies today?”

items.fail: Arranging a same-day surgery appointment for a baby with reported apnoea.
items.why: It delays emergency care and exposes the baby and other patients to risk.
items.fix: 999 ambulance, with interim advice and a call-back.

items.fail: Telling the mother to go to hospital but ignoring that she has a toddler and no car.
items.why: An unworkable plan is not a safe plan.
items.fix: Ask “what would make this hard?” and solve it together.

After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: 999 ambulance now — no home-care or next-day plan; agrees who rings, what to say and childcare for Mariam; explains why in plain words without blame.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “he’s sleepier than normal”, the hesitation at “anything else?” (the pause in breathing lies behind it) and “my husband can’t just leave work”.
Idea (sister’s cold, chest infection, needs antibiotics); concern (what she saw at 3 am, being judged, who minds Mariam); expectation (Calpol advice, not hospital).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Underneath: she is frightened by what she saw at 3 am but worried she will be judged as an over-anxious mum or will “waste an ambulance”. She also worries about who will look after Mariam — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
